Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Statistics & Visualization
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 13, Statistics and Visualization. In Module 12, we focused on cleaning and validating data. Now we are ready to ask what the cleaned data is actually telling us.

Statistics gives us numerical summaries. Visualization helps us see distributions, differences, trends, and relationships that may be difficult to notice in a table.

[tts-break]

The goal is not to calculate every statistic or create as many charts as possible. The goal is to choose the statistic and visual that answer the analytical question clearly.

Throughout this module, we will use a small order dataset and examine it from several perspectives.

By the end, you should be able to describe numeric data, compare groups, study relationships, choose an appropriate chart, and write interpretations that match the strength of the evidence.

slides.title: From Cleaning & EDA to Statistics & Visualization
slides.transcript:
Module 12 answered the question, can we trust the data?

Module 13 asks the next question: what does the data tell us?

Once values are consistently coded and obvious quality problems are addressed, we can use statistics and charts with much more confidence.

[tts-break]

We will move from descriptive summaries into distributions, group comparisons, scatter plots, correlation, and a simple introduction to confidence intervals.

Statistics and visualization work best together. A summary table gives us exact values. A chart makes patterns easier to see.

After this module, Module 14 will introduce machine learning and external data. The ideas here are important preparation because machine learning also depends on understanding distributions, relationships, and variation before fitting a model.

slides.title: Our working dataset
slides.transcript:
For this module, we will use one small cleaned dataset with region, channel, amount, and satisfaction.

Region and channel are categorical variables. Amount is a numeric variable. Satisfaction is a numeric rating that we will use carefully for introductory examples.

Before choosing a statistic or chart, identify the type of variable you are working with.

[tts-break]

Variable type matters because different questions require different tools.

If you want to understand the distribution of amount, a histogram may help.

If you want to compare average amount across regions, a grouped summary or bar chart may be useful.

If you want to examine the relationship between two numeric variables, a scatter plot is usually a better choice.

The question and variable types should guide the method, not the other way around.

slides.title: Descriptive statistics
slides.transcript:
Descriptive statistics summarize the main characteristics of the data you currently have.

The mean describes the arithmetic average. The median describes the middle value. Standard deviation describes how spread out values are around the mean. Quartiles describe positions within the ordered data.

Run the code and inspect the describe output for order amount.

[tts-break]

Notice that no single statistic tells the whole story.

Two datasets can have the same mean but very different variability.

A mean can also be affected by extreme values, while the median is usually more resistant.

A good descriptive summary therefore uses several measures together.

When you report statistics, always connect the number to the variable and units. Saying the mean is ninety is less informative than saying the mean order amount is ninety dollars.

slides.title: Mean versus median
slides.transcript:
The mean and median are both measures of center, but they behave differently when extreme values are present.

Look at the first set of numbers. The values are balanced, so both the mean and median are thirty.

Now replace the largest value with four hundred. The median stays at thirty, but the mean increases dramatically.

[tts-break]

This does not mean the mean is bad. It means the mean answers a different question and is sensitive to every value.

For variables such as income, home prices, hospital charges, or transaction amounts, distributions are often skewed. In those cases, the median may better represent a typical observation.

A useful EDA habit is to compare mean and median instead of reporting only one of them.

If they are very different, investigate the distribution and possible extreme values.

slides.title: Visualize a distribution with a histogram
slides.transcript:
A histogram helps us understand how a numeric variable is distributed.

The horizontal axis represents numeric ranges, called bins. The vertical axis shows how many observations fall inside each range.

Run the Python code and examine the distribution of order amounts.

[tts-break]

Look for the general shape. Is it roughly symmetric? Is it skewed? Are there gaps or clusters? Is one observation far away from the others?

Also experiment with the number of bins. A histogram is a summary, so the appearance can change when the bin width changes.

That is why you should not overinterpret very small details in one histogram.

The main purpose is to see the overall distribution and compare what you see with the descriptive statistics from the previous slides.

slides.title: Boxplots summarize distributions
slides.transcript:
A boxplot provides a compact visual summary of a numeric distribution.

The line inside the box represents the median. The box covers the middle fifty percent of the data, from Q1 to Q3. The whiskers extend beyond the box, and points beyond the whiskers may be flagged as potential outliers.

[tts-break]

Boxplots become especially useful when we place several groups side by side.

Run the code and compare order amount across North, South, and West.

Look at the medians and the spread within each region.

Do not focus only on which group has the highest maximum.

A useful comparison asks whether one group tends to be higher overall, whether one group has more variability, and whether any unusual values appear.

The visual should support the same interpretation as your numerical summary.

slides.title: Compare groups with summary statistics
slides.transcript:
Grouped statistics let us compare categories numerically.

In this example, we calculate count, mean, median, and standard deviation for each region.

Count is important because a group with very few observations can produce an unstable average.

[tts-break]

Mean and median describe the center in different ways, while standard deviation tells us about within-group variability.

Run the code and compare the regions.

Ask whether the mean and median tell a similar story. If they are far apart, the group may contain skewness or unusual values.

Also be careful not to make strong population claims from a very small teaching dataset.

At this stage, we are practicing descriptive comparison. Formal inference requires additional assumptions and methods.

slides.title: Bar charts for categorical comparisons
slides.transcript:
A bar chart is useful for comparing values across categories.

In the example, we first calculate the average order amount for each region, then plot those regional averages.

The categories are on one axis, and the summary value is represented by bar height.

[tts-break]

A bar chart is different from a histogram.

A histogram shows the distribution of one numeric variable across numeric ranges. A bar chart compares discrete categories.

When bar length represents magnitude, the numeric axis should usually begin at zero so the visual difference is not exaggerated.

Keep labels readable and avoid unnecessary decoration.

The purpose of the chart is to make the category comparison easier to understand than the table alone.

slides.title: Scatter plots for numeric relationships
slides.transcript:
A scatter plot is one of the most useful visuals when both variables are numeric.

Each point represents one observation. One variable is placed on the horizontal axis and the other on the vertical axis.

The pattern of points can tell us about direction, shape, strength, clusters, and unusual observations.

[tts-break]

Run the example and look at amount versus satisfaction.

Before calculating any correlation coefficient, describe what you see.

Do higher amounts generally appear with higher satisfaction? Is the pattern roughly linear? Are there unusual points?

This visual inspection is important because a single number can hide nonlinear patterns or influential observations.

A good workflow is plot first, summarize second, interpret last.

slides.title: Correlation
slides.transcript:
Correlation gives us a numerical summary of the linear relationship between two numeric variables.

Pearson correlation ranges from minus one to plus one.

A positive value means the variables tend to increase together. A negative value means one tends to decrease as the other increases. A value near zero means there is little linear association.

[tts-break]

Run the code and compare the coefficient with the scatter plot from the previous slide.

The word linear is important. A correlation near zero does not prove that there is no relationship. The relationship could be curved or affected by other structure in the data.

Also remember that correlation is not causation.

It describes association in the observed data. It does not prove that changing one variable will cause the other variable to change.

slides.title: Correlation can be misleading
slides.transcript:
Correlation is useful, but it can be misleading when we ignore the shape and context of the data.

A curved relationship may have a low linear correlation. One extreme observation can change the coefficient dramatically. Subgroups can create or hide a pattern. Restricted ranges can also weaken an apparent relationship.

[tts-break]

This is why correlation should not be the first and only analysis.

A better sequence is to plot the variables, inspect outliers and groups, calculate the coefficient, and then interpret it in context.

When you see a correlation, ask what the scatter plot looks like and whether another variable could be affecting both measurements.

Good statistical reasoning combines the number with the data-generating process.

slides.title: A simple confidence interval idea
slides.transcript:
Descriptive statistics summarize the sample we have. But often we are interested in a larger population.

A sample mean is an estimate of the population mean, and that estimate contains uncertainty.

A confidence interval gives us a range around the estimate using a statistical procedure.

[tts-break]

In this introductory example, we use the sample mean plus or minus one point nine six times the standard error.

Focus on the idea more than the formula.

If the sample is small or highly variable, the interval tends to be wider. With more information and less variability, the estimate can become more precise.

This simple formula relies on assumptions, so it is not a universal rule.

The goal here is to introduce the idea that sample statistics are estimates, not exact population truths.

slides.title: Choose the right visual
slides.transcript:
Choosing a chart should begin with the analytical question.

If you want to understand one numeric distribution, use a histogram.

If you want to compare numeric distributions across groups, a boxplot may help.

If you want to compare categories by count or summary value, use a bar chart.

If you want to study the relationship between two numeric variables, use a scatter plot.

[tts-break]

For measurements across ordered time, a line chart is often appropriate.

And sometimes a table is better than a chart when readers need exact values.

There is no single best chart for every dataset.

The best visual is the one that makes the relevant comparison or pattern easiest to understand without distorting the evidence.

slides.title: Make charts easier to read
slides.transcript:
A chart can be technically correct and still communicate poorly.

Good visualization reduces unnecessary work for the reader.

Use a specific title. Label the axes. Include units when they matter. Keep category labels readable. Avoid decorations that do not support interpretation.

[tts-break]

Be especially careful with scales.

For example, truncating a bar chart axis can make a small difference look very large.

Three-dimensional effects can also distort the apparent size of values.

Color should have a purpose, such as distinguishing meaningful groups, not simply decorating the chart.

Remember that design choices can influence what the reader notices.

A strong analytical chart is clear, honest, and focused on the question being answered.

slides.title: Line charts for time trends
slides.transcript:
Line charts are useful when observations have a meaningful order in time.

In the example, the horizontal axis contains dates and the vertical axis contains sales.

Connecting the points helps us see whether the series is increasing, decreasing, or fluctuating over time.

[tts-break]

Before plotting, make sure the dates are sorted.

Also think about the time interval. Daily, weekly, and monthly summaries can reveal different patterns.

Do not use a line simply because it looks attractive. A line implies continuity and order.

It makes sense for days, months, or years, but not for unrelated categories such as region names.

Run the example and look for the general direction of the trend rather than focusing on every small change.

slides.title: Mini statistics report
slides.transcript:
A useful analytical report combines a clear question, numerical summaries, an appropriate visual, and a short interpretation.

The example asks how order amount differs across regions.

We calculate count, mean, and median, then create a boxplot to compare the group distributions.

[tts-break]

Read the table and chart together.

The table provides exact values. The boxplot helps you see differences in center and spread.

If the table and chart seem to tell different stories, investigate why.

For example, an extreme value may increase the mean while the median stays relatively stable.

A good report does not end with code output.

End with a sentence that explains what the evidence suggests and any limitations that affect the interpretation.

slides.title: Interpret carefully
slides.transcript:
Strong analysis uses language that matches the strength of the evidence.

If West has the highest mean in this sample, say exactly that.

Do not turn a sample pattern into a universal statement such as West customers always spend more.

Similarly, if two variables are correlated, say they are associated in the data.

Do not automatically say that one causes the other.

[tts-break]

Words matter because they communicate how certain the conclusion is.

Phrases such as in this sample, appears higher, is associated with, or may indicate are often appropriate for descriptive analysis.

Causal claims require stronger study designs, assumptions, and evidence.

A good analyst is not someone who makes the strongest statement possible. A good analyst makes the strongest statement that the evidence actually supports.

slides.title: Practice challenge
slides.transcript:
Now you will create a small statistical story using the starter dataset.

Begin by describing the amount column and comparing the mean with the median.

Then create a histogram and summarize amount by region.

Create one group-comparison chart, followed by a scatter plot of amount and satisfaction.

Finally, calculate the correlation.

[tts-break]

Do not stop with the code.

Write three interpretation sentences.

One sentence should describe the distribution. One should compare the groups. One should describe the relationship between the two numeric variables.

Check that your written statements match both the statistics and the visualizations.

The goal is to practice moving from data to evidence and then from evidence to careful interpretation.

slides.title: Module 13 wrap-up
slides.transcript:
Module 13 combined statistics and visualization to help us describe and communicate data more clearly.

You used mean, median, standard deviation, quartiles, and grouped summaries. You created histograms, boxplots, bar charts, scatter plots, and line charts. You also introduced correlation and the idea of uncertainty through a simple confidence interval.

[tts-break]

The most important lesson is that numbers and visuals should support the same analytical question.

In Module 14, we will take one more step. We will introduce machine learning by connecting simple algebra to learned relationships, features, numeric vectors, train and test data, prediction, and evaluation.

That final module is designed as a bridge into the machine learning course you will take next semester.
